burdens.description: Establish that belief in the Christian God is reasonable.
burdens.successCriteria: Provide a non-question-begging route from publicly assessable premises to the Christian God's existence or to justified belief in that existence.

burdens.description: Establish that truth, logic, knowledge, and reasoning require the Christian God.
burdens.successCriteria: Explain the dependence relation and show both that Christianity supplies the required foundation and that relevant alternatives cannot.

burdens.description: Defend divine revelation as a reliable epistemic route.
burdens.successCriteria: Explain how fallible people can identify genuine revelation, distinguish it from rivals, and receive truth without circularly assuming the source.

burdens.description: Show that non-Christian induction lacks adequate warrant while Christian revelation supplies it.
burdens.successCriteria: Identify the defect in probabilistic induction and demonstrate how revelation improves predictive warrant without merely asserting certainty.

burdens.description: State and defend an appropriate standard for reasonable belief.
burdens.successCriteria: Connect validity, evidential support, and proportionate confidence to belief while distinguishing reasonableness from absolute certainty.

burdens.description: Defend modest epistemic starting points against the charge of self-defeat.
burdens.successCriteria: Explain why using reason, senses, and shared experience is practically or epistemically warranted without claiming inaccessible ultimate certainty.

burdens.description: Test whether the pro case actually demonstrates its asserted foundation.
burdens.successCriteria: Identify missing inferential bridges, burden shifts, or circularity and directly request the demonstration needed to repair them.

burdens.description: Challenge the discriminatory power of claimed revelation.
burdens.successCriteria: Show how materially similar rival claims arise and require a publicly usable method that selects Christianity rather than merely restating it.

sections.title: Reasonable belief and the motion-level burden
sections.weightRationale: The debate formally asks whether belief is reasonable, so each side's governing criterion and initial burden posture shape every later exchange.

moves.speaker: Sye Ten Bruggencate

moves.summary: Presents a valid syllogistic form whose decisive premise is that God exists.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the pro side's explicit opening argument and states the central premise later challenged throughout the debate.

passA.rationale: The form is valid, clear, and central to the motion, so coherence, responsiveness, and relevance score strongly. The move itself supplies almost no warrant for premise two, however, and treats the truth of that premise more confidently than the support yet given permits.

evidence.basis: The syllogism is stated explicitly through 00:02:22, but the decisive premise, 'God exists,' is only announced as the coming point of dispute.

passB.rationale: At 00:02:02.960 the syllogism is explicit and valid in form, and it directly addresses reasonableness. Its decisive existence premise is simply declared true, however, so strong structure and relevance cannot discharge the central evidential burden; the later claim that the debate is thereby over is substantially overconfident.

moves.summary: Rejects evidential adjudication by the listener and asserts universal knowledge of God as epistemically prior.
moves.selectionRationale: This directly states why the pro side declines the con side's requested public-evidence procedure.

passA.rationale: The move clearly explains the pro side's refusal of the con's evidential procedure, but the court analogy does not show that public evidence is epistemically illegitimate. The universal-knowledge assertion is unsupported and markedly overconfident, leaving the motion's reasonableness burden largely undischarged.

evidence.basis: From 00:21:20 to 00:21:44, the request for evidence is rejected because the listener would be made judge, followed by the assertion that everyone already knows God exists.

passB.rationale: At 00:21:20.320 the response plainly states the claimed priority of God and explains why public evidence is refused. Yet universal God-knowledge and the listener's lack of adjudicative standing are asserted through the very revelation under challenge, leaving the inferential bridge and warrant absent while imputing suppressed knowledge to opponents.

adjudication.rationale: The turn directly explains why public evidence is refused, supporting slightly more responsiveness than Pass A allowed. It nevertheless substitutes asserted divine priority and universal God-knowledge for the requested warrant, so it remains mixed-to-weak on relevance and does not reach Pass B's burden score.

finalResolution.rationale: The turn directly explains why public evidence is refused, supporting slightly more responsiveness than Pass A allowed. It nevertheless substitutes asserted divine priority and universal God-knowledge for the requested warrant, so it remains mixed-to-weak on relevance and does not reach Pass B's burden score.

sections.title: Ultimate reality, solipsism, and fallible access
sections.weightRationale: The brain-in-a-vat challenge dominates the opening and cross-examination and tests whether modest fallibilism is self-defeating.

moves.summary: Claims ultimate truth requires revelation and characterizes professed disbelief as suppression of known divine reality.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the constructive bridge from skepticism about ultimate reality to the asserted necessity of revelation.

passA.rationale: This is highly relevant because it states the intended bridge from skepticism to revelation, but it does not establish the dependence relation or a way to discriminate genuine revelation. Treating disagreement as suppressed knowledge substitutes motive attribution for warrant and weakens calibration and charity.

evidence.basis: From 00:09:49 to 00:10:14, ultimate truth is said to require divine revelation, while professed atheism is characterized as suppression of known truth.

passB.rationale: At 00:09:49.440 revelation is offered as the bridge from hard skepticism to truth, which is highly relevant to the locked transcendental burden. The move does not establish why truth requires ultimate access, how revelation supplies it, or why dissent is suppression; those are asserted with certainty and adverse motive attribution.

sections.title: Logical absolutes and worldview accounting
sections.weightRationale: Whether logic needs and receives a specifically Christian foundation is the core transcendental claim and carries the largest single section weight.

moves.speaker: Sye Ten Bruggencate
moves.sourceExcerpt: if biochemical reactions are all that you are thinking then all that you can say is that what you perceive to be logical true and Absolut necessary is nothing more than the result of chemical reactions in your brain if Matt's worldview is true then our thoughts our brains are just evolved meat machines and our thoughts are the byproduct of the chemical reactions in our evolved Brains you can't get truth from that
moves.summary: Argues that a biochemical account of thought cannot yield logical necessity or truth.
moves.selectionRationale: This supplies the pro side's most developed negative argument against a naturalistic account of reasoning.

passA.rationale: The move addresses the core accounting burden and makes its negative case intelligible, but it does not show why a physical causal history prevents representational truth or logical competence. The beverage-fizz and 'evolved meat machine' framing is a weak reconstruction of a naturalistic account, lowering warrant and charity.

evidence.basis: From 00:22:23 to 00:23:16, natural thought is analogized to undirected fizz and the biochemical origin of a thought is treated as precluding truth.

passB.rationale: At 00:22:23.240 the move clearly raises the important normativity problem for a wholly biochemical account of thought. It does not show why a causal description of cognition precludes true content or valid inference, and it compresses the opposing view into 'meat machines' without engaging possible naturalistic accounts of representation or normativity.

adjudication.rationale: The move raises a real normativity question but supplies no bridge from physical causation to the impossibility of truth-bearing content. Pass B's warrant score is better anchored to the rubric's effectively unsupported fact-dependent band.

finalResolution.rationale: The move raises a real normativity question but supplies no bridge from physical causation to the impossibility of truth-bearing content. Pass B's warrant score is better anchored to the rubric's effectively unsupported fact-dependent band.

sections.title: Reason, circularity, and induction
sections.weightRationale: These exchanges test whether ordinary epistemic practice is viciously circular and whether probabilistic induction needs revealed certainty.

moves.selectionRationale: This is the clearest live statement of the circularity objection and includes the con side's practical-necessity reply.

evidence.basis: From 00:39:36 to 00:40:26, the pro side elicits that reason is used in assessing reason's effective track record and identifies the resulting epistemic circularity.

passB.rationale: At 00:39:36.720 the circularity question is sharply stated and exposes that reason's track record is itself assessed through reasoning. It materially advances the foundations challenge, but it does not establish that this unavoidable epistemic circularity is vicious or that revelation avoids an analogous problem; the excerpt's mixed turns lower attribution confidence.

sections.title: Revelation, scripture, and rival religious claims
sections.weightRationale: Because revelation is offered as the epistemic solution, its accessibility, corrigibility, and discriminatory power are load-bearing.

moves.selectionRationale: This consequentially defines the limits of public testing permitted for the revelation offered as the epistemic foundation.

passA.rationale: The response clearly states its presuppositional policy but does not answer the concrete challenge or provide a public reliability test. evidence.basis: At 01:16:38–01:17:24, a concrete proposed scriptural error is met with a refusal to put scripture's truth to an atheist's test.

passB.rationale: At 01:16:35.200 the speaker clearly states a presupposition-sensitive refusal to let nonbelievers test scripture. adjudication.rationale: The presupposition-sensitive refusal is internally intelligible as a policy, but it declines the concrete reliability test and supplies no public discriminator for revelation. That is a very weak response to the live burden, closer to Pass A than Pass B.

finalResolution.rationale: The presupposition-sensitive refusal is internally intelligible as a policy, but it declines the concrete reliability test and supplies no public discriminator for revelation. That is a very weak response to the live burden, closer to Pass A than Pass B.
